facts.fact: Name for the term: "khí CO2"
Name for the term: "CO2 trong thủy sinh"
Plants use CO2 as a basic building block for growth. Light, fertilizer and CO2 must stay in balance.
In photosynthesis, plants turn CO2 and water into sugars and release oxygen.
Carbon makes up almost half of a plant's dry mass.
Without added CO2, an aquarium holds on average about 0.5 mg/L of CO2. Natural waters with dense plant growth can reach up to 50 mg/l.
Air contains about 400 ppm CO2, but water typically holds only about 2 to 4 mg/l, which is why plants may need extra CO2.
Some dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, so a moderate addition lowers the pH into the slightly acidic range.
Fish and invertebrates get rid of CO2 through their gills by diffusion. This works only if the water holds clearly less CO2 than their blood.
At high CO2 levels, animals cannot release the gas and so cannot take up oxygen. In the worst case they suffocate even though oxygen is present.
Fast-growing plants such as Rotala need more added CO2. So do strong light and dense planting.
A tank under 20 lít may have enough natural CO2. Tanks of 60 lít or more often lack it.
Too much CO2 in fish shows as lethargy, poor appetite, loss of consciousness and gasping at the surface.
With too much CO2, fish swim sluggishly and rise to the surface to breathe. If this goes on, fish can die.
Signs of too little CO2 include leaves turning yellow, slowed growth, and algae or bacteria blooms.
On a drop checker, green means the right level, yellow means too much CO2 and dark blue means too little.
Plants pearling is a sign that the water is saturated with oxygen.
CO2 can build up from overdosing through an injection system.
At night plants respire and release CO2, which adds to the buildup.
Some kits inject too much gas as the cylinder nears empty.
Low dissolved oxygen makes fish more sensitive to CO2.
Errors in pH/KH test kit readings can hide dangerous CO2 levels.
CO2 can harm fish if pH drops too quickly or if the setup cuts off oxygen.
For a CO2 overdose, do a large water change with dechlorinated water at the tank's temperature. This is the quickest and most effective fix.
An air stone or surface agitation helps against excess CO2, but less than a water change.
Most fish and invertebrates tolerate about 30 ppm (mg/l) of CO2. The page cites an FDACS recommendation of under 32 ppm for aquatic livestock.
Safe CO2 levels are higher when dissolved oxygen is high and lower when it is low.
pH 6.6 with 4 KH corresponds to about 32 ppm CO2.
Dennerle recommends about 20 mg/L of CO2 for planted tanks, checked with a continuous test so this limit is not exceeded.
Start a pressurized system at about 1 bubble per second, a deliberately light dose to keep fish safe, then increase the rate until plants pearl.
Plants take at least 24 hours to respond, so wait three days between bubble-rate adjustments.
Aquarium Co-Op does not chase 30 ppm with drop checkers. It watches how the plants respond instead.
A pH of 6.5 to 7.5 is usually ideal for most plants and fish.
Step 1: Screw the regulator onto the CO2 cylinder.
Step 2: Fill the bubble counter with water or mineral oil and attach airline tubing to its lid.
Step 3: Run the tubing to the diffuser at the bottom of the tank.
Step 4 (optional): Fit a check valve in the line near the tank rim.
Step 5: Connect the solenoid cable to its power adapter, plug the adapter into a timer, and plug the timer into an outlet.
Turn CO2 on 1–2 hours before the light and off 1 hour before the light shuts off.
Use a two-stage regulator for steadier flow.
Cylinder sizes: 2.5–5 lb for tanks up to 20 gallons, 5 lb for 25–40 gallons, and 10 lb for 55 gallons or more.
Bio CO2 systems use microorganisms that break down organic material to make CO2. They suit tanks up to 100 liters.
Turn off CO2 at night, because plants respire then and release CO2 instead of using it.
Turn off CO2 at night, or use an automatic system that follows the time of day.
Change the CO2 cylinder before the gas runs very low.
Aim for a darker green on the drop checker rather than yellowish-green. In large tanks use more than one checker. In small tanks, move it around.
Add an air stone for surface agitation. The bubble rate may need a slight increase to make up for lost CO2.
Instead of adding CO2, keepers can grow plants that need little of it, such as Anubias.
Expecting CO2 alone to stop algae is a mistake. Too much light or fertilizer for the amount of CO2 (or the reverse) brings algae.
More light needs more fertilizer and more CO2, or algae will spread.
Cutting surface agitation to save CO2 also cuts oxygen and can make fish gasp.
Don't use paintball cylinders. The regulator needs standard cylinders with CGA320 threads.
Mounting the diffuser high means the bubbles don't dissolve. Place it as low as possible and clean it when algae clogs it.
CO2 slowly degrades plastic check valves, so they should not be used indefinitely.
Dennerle advises against using CO2 to force a very high pH sharply down.
Common mistakes: overdosing CO2, leaving it running at night, not monitoring the level with a meter, and ignoring refill and upkeep costs.
If CO2 is too high and pH drops too far, plants are stressed, and fish can be stressed if pH falls too low.
Liquid CO2 ("dung dịch CO2 lỏng") should not be overdosed.
Vietnamese shop pages name CO2 equipment "bình CO2" (cylinder), "bộ đếm giọt CO2" (bubble counter), "van điều chỉnh" (regulator) and "máy đo nồng độ CO2 (drop checker)".
Products named on a Vietnamese shop's page: "dung dịch CO2 lỏng", "viên CO2" and "hệ thống CO2 tự động".
Dennerle answers "Does my aquarium work without CO2?" with "yes and no": some hardy plants manage with little CO2 but grow better with more.
